review:
A film so committed to its mechanism that it forgets to give anyone a reason to care whether the mechanism works. Christopher Nolan has built an extraordinary machine here — the inverted car chase on the Tallinn highway is genuinely unlike anything else in the medium — and then bolted it to characters who exist mainly to explain it.

The explanations are the problem. Roughly a third of the dialogue is exposition about entropy, delivered at volume over a score that seems actively hostile to consonants. The mixing has been defended as a deliberate choice. It may well be. It is still a choice that makes the film harder to follow than its plot warrants, and the plot warrants quite a lot.

Washington is charismatic and given nothing; Pattinson is charming and given a secret he cannot play until the last ten minutes. Debicki comes closest to a real performance, largely because her character wants something a person could plausibly want. Everyone else wants to prevent the end of the world, which turns out to be surprisingly abstract.

Admirable, cold, and strangely forgettable for a film this loud. The set pieces deserve a better story around them.
